newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Guam seeks representation in U.S. govt.
newsitem.headline: Guam seeks representation in U.S. govt.

text.p: The governor of the U.S. Pacific territory of Guam on Friday demanded better representation in the U.S. government, saying its people wanted to determine their own future.
"Today, we the people of Guam are sending our own message to the U.S. Federal Government," Carl Gutierrez said in a statement sent to news agencies in Manila.

"Here we stand, American citizens who are denied meaningful participation in democracy. We cannot vote for President. We have no vote in Congress. We are a possession and are denied any say in our future.

"Make no mistake about it, we are a colony, a colony of a nation dedicated to ending colonialism," Gutierrez said in the statement, which was to be delivered to the aircraft carrier USS Independence when it calls at Guam's Apra Harbour on Friday.
Native Chamorros are asking for right of self-determination as well as rights to their ancestral lands, Gutierrez said.
"The self-determination we seek has not occurred because there are some who would deny us a say in the future of our own island," he said without elaborating.
"If we are good enough to host military bases, planes, nuclear weapons and ships...then we are at least owed the political dignity we seek," the statement added.
Guam has been pushing for greater autonomy since 1988. But its efforts have been blocked by previous administrations.
The proposed Guam Commonwealth Act would give the territory control over immigration to the island as well as the authority to enforce labour regulations.

The immigration provision is controversial because some U.S. officials fear that local authorities could import thousands of low-wage labourers from Asia and subject them to poor treatment, a recent report in the Washington Post said.
Guam, a tiny tropical island in the Western Pacific, has 140,000 residents and marks its centennial as a U.S. possesison next year.
